text: Barring members of Congress and the president from owning or trading individual stocks would reduce the use of public office for private gain.
bottom_line: The conflict is documented and the disclosure regime demonstrably fails. Whether a ban removes the conflict or relocates it into spouses, partnerships and the revolving door is the open question. It is one of three load-bearing components all sitting at the neutral start, and while they sit there any one of them caps what this page can read, however far the evidence carries the argument.
hook: Members of Congress trade in the industries their own committees oversee, and the penalty for filing late is a $200 fee that is routinely waived.
question: Would barring members of Congress and the president from holding individual stocks reduce the use of office for private gain, or move the money somewhere the rule cannot see?
form: (Officials' holdings currently influence official decisions) AND (removing the holdings removes the influence rather than relocating it) AND (a ban can be enacted and enforced). The normative component, that reducing conflicts is worth a narrower candidate pool, is separable.

text: Barring the president and members of Congress from giving any official government function to a family member would reduce the use of public office for private gain.
bottom_line: The legal gap is documented and the supervision problem is real. The page turns on whether a bar removes the conflict or converts a disclosed adviser into an undisclosed one. All three load-bearing components sit at the neutral start, so nothing has been established here yet and nothing is capping anything: the work is to argue them.
hook: The anti-nepotism statute stops at the White House door.
question: Would barring the president and members of Congress from handing official functions to relatives reduce the use of office for private gain?
form: (Relatives in official roles produce conflicts that ordinary supervision cannot check) AND (a bar removes those conflicts rather than driving them out of view) AND (Congress can impose the bar on the White House). The third component is where the legal fight is.

text: Requiring the president and members of Congress to publish their tax returns would reduce the use of public office for private gain.
bottom_line: The documentary claim is the strongest part: returns do carry conflict-relevant facts the disclosure form omits. What nobody can show is that publishing them changes anything. All three load-bearing components sit at the neutral start, so what this page needs is not more evidence for the conclusion but an argument for each of its parts.
hook: Every president from Carter through Obama published tax returns without a law requiring it.
question: Would requiring the president and members of Congress to publish their tax returns reduce the use of office for private gain, or expose spouses and partners for little in return?
form: (Returns contain conflict-relevant information the disclosure form lacks) AND (publishing it changes behavior or enables a check) AND (a publication requirement can be imposed). The first is documentary, the second is contested, the third is narrower than the usual objection assumes.

text: Letting Congress overturn a presidential pardon by a two-thirds vote of both chambers would reduce the use of the pardon power for private gain.
bottom_line: The gap is real: clemency is the only federal power with no check, and grants to the president's own circle are documented in both parties. All three load-bearing components sit at the neutral start, so any one of them caps the page. The one to argue first is not the constitutional objection but whether an override could ever be exercised at a two-thirds threshold against a president whose own party holds a third of either chamber.
hook: A pardon is final the moment it is signed, and no other executive power has so little standing over it.
question: Would letting Congress overturn a pardon by a two-thirds vote of both chambers reduce the use of the pardon power for private gain?
form: (Some pardons are granted for the president's private benefit) AND (a congressional override would deter or reverse those grants) AND (an override can be enacted). The third component is legal rather than empirical, and it is the one most likely to hold this page down once all three have been argued.

text: Public office should not be usable for private gain.
bottom_line: Held nearly universally at this level of generality, which is why the argument always moves to the specific rules below it.
hook: Every federal ethics statute since the 1962 reforms rests on one sentence, and the sentence itself is rarely argued.
question: Should public office be unusable for private gain, without exception, or are there gains an officeholder may keep?

text: Every federal ethics statute since the 1962 conflict-of-interest reforms rests on this principle, so rejecting it would unsettle the whole body of law rather than one rule.
bottom_line: True as legal history; that is a weaker claim than the principle itself.

text: If office can be used for private gain, decisions go to whoever pays the most rather than to whoever is right, which is the definition of a government that does not work.
bottom_line: The mechanism is right in the extreme case; the size of the effect at low levels of self-dealing is not established here.

text: It is the rare principle with supermajority agreement across parties: 86 percent of registered voters backed a congressional stock trading ban, including 87 percent of Republicans and 88 percent of Democrats.
bottom_line: Well measured for the stock trading case; it says what people want, not what is right.

text: Stated at this level the principle decides nothing, because every real dispute is about what counts as "gain" and what counts as "using" the office.
bottom_line: A real objection to using the principle as a decision rule, not to holding it.

text: Taken literally it would bar anyone who owns anything from serving, which would leave office to people with no stake in the country they govern.
bottom_line: A reductio that the drafted versions of these rules already avoid.

text: Members regularly trade in the industries their own committees oversee, which puts a private financial stake on both sides of decisions they control.
bottom_line: The overlap is documented; what it causes is the contested part.

text: Disclosure has failed as a check: 78 members of one Congress filed late under the STOCK Act, the standard penalty is a $200 fee that is routinely waived, and no member has faced a serious sanction.
bottom_line: The enforcement record is strong evidence; it shows the reporting regime is unenforced, not that trades were corrupt.

text: A holdings ban removes the conflict itself instead of asking the public to police thousands of individual trades after the fact.
bottom_line: The strongest structural argument on the page: it changes what has to be proven.

text: The Federal Reserve barred its own policymakers from holding individual stocks in 2022 and kept functioning and kept hiring, which shows a comparable institution can operate under the rule.
bottom_line: A live natural experiment in a nearby institution, with a real scope objection.

text: Trading on a closed briefing is almost impossible to prosecute, so the only rule that can actually be enforced is one that does not require proving what an official knew.
bottom_line: The enforcement asymmetry is real; it is evidence about provability, not about guilt.

text: The best-identified studies of actual returns find congressional portfolios underperform the market, which is hard to square with a systematic insider advantage.
bottom_line: The aggregate finding is solid and the rebuttal is that aggregates are the wrong place to look.

text: A ban on the official leaves the conflict in place through spouses, dependent children, private partnerships, real estate and crypto, none of which most proposals reach.
bottom_line: A real drafting objection that the Fed template already answers in part.

text: Forced divestiture imposes real costs on officials of ordinary means and narrows who can afford to serve.
bottom_line: The cost is real and largely fixable in drafting; the rebuttal is stronger than the argument.

text: Members keep the property rights of other citizens, and a ban restricts a lawful activity because of the job someone holds.
bottom_line: Weakest of the four: the restriction is common elsewhere in government and the office is voluntary.

text: Congress will not enforce a ban on itself, so the statute would put a symbol in place of the enforcement reform that could work.
bottom_line: The best argument against: it predicts the failure mode from the closest precedent.

text: Senators' stock purchases beat the market by about 85 basis points a month, roughly 10 percent a year, over 1993 to 1998.
bottom_line: Methodologically solid for its period; its period is the problem.

text: Trades placed before legislative events earned abnormal returns of about 3 to 5 percent over 2014 to 2021.
bottom_line: The most direct answer to the underperformance studies, and the newest, which cuts both ways.

text: 78 members of the 117th Congress violated the STOCK Act's disclosure deadlines.
bottom_line: Accurate as a count of filing failures; frequently oversold as a count of misconduct.

text: 131 federal judges heard 685 cases involving companies in which they or their families held stock, over 2010 to 2018.
bottom_line: Strong evidence about disclosure regimes generally; one institution removed from the belief.

text: Federal Reserve officials have been barred from holding individual stocks, sector funds, individual bonds, crypto and derivatives since May 2022, with preclearance and a one-year holding period.
bottom_line: Establishes that the rule is workable; says little yet about its long-run costs.

text: Congressional portfolios underperformed market benchmarks by roughly 2 to 3 percent a year over 2004 to 2008.
bottom_line: The strongest single piece of evidence against, and its known weakness is that averages hide tails.

text: No evidence that members of Congress outperformed the market over 2012 to 2020, the period after the STOCK Act.
bottom_line: Directly on point for the trading-advantage claim; silent on the voting-conflict claim.

text: Five years after a ban takes effect, individual equity holdings reported by members fall to near zero and no trading scandal originates in Congress.
bottom_line: Pending, and the metric is gameable in a way the prediction should name.

text: Public trust in Congress five years after a ban is higher than the pre-ban trend predicted.
bottom_line: Weakly diagnostic: a lot of noise for one signal.

text: A jurisdiction that adopts a holdings ban shows conflicted votes falling relative to comparable bodies that did not.
bottom_line: The single most informative study nobody has run.

text: Reported conflicts migrate to spouse accounts and private partnerships, leaving the total number of conflict complaints unchanged.
bottom_line: The most likely way the belief fails, and the one the drafting can answer.

text: The share of incoming members whose wealth is in the top 1 percent rises after a ban.
bottom_line: Testable from existing data, and the base rate makes a large move unlikely.

text: Post-reform studies continue to find no abnormal returns, so there is no trading advantage for a ban to remove.
bottom_line: Would weaken one branch of the tree and leave the other standing.

text: Members stop voting on industries in which they hold a personal stake.
bottom_line: Mechanically near-certain in direction, contested in size.

text: Officials stop placing trades ahead of government announcements.
bottom_line: Direction certain, magnitude resting on a contested base rate.

text: Voters can tell a compromised official from a clean one without an investigation.
bottom_line: The benefit most often claimed and the least supported by the record.

text: Officials get one rule they can follow without a lawyer instead of a reporting regime they violate by accident.
bottom_line: Plausible and small; the Fed rule suggests the saving is partly offset.

text: Officials sell holdings on a schedule they did not choose and pay tax on the gains.
bottom_line: Real and largely solvable in drafting.

text: Mid-career professionals with savings in individual equities decline to run.
bottom_line: The mechanism is real; the affected group is narrower than the argument implies.

text: Officeholders lose income they currently earn from trading on their position.
bottom_line: A cost that only exists to the extent the belief's own premise is true, and it falls on an interest almost nobody defends.

text: Members divest or move holdings into diversified funds within the compliance window.
Filing volume falls because there are fewer transactions to report.
Conflict complaints shift from trading to family and outside business interests.
The rule becomes unremarkable, as judicial and executive branch holding rules did.
Officials' financial holdings currently influence how they vote and what they say.
bottom_line: Documented as correlation, not established as influence. This is the load-bearing claim the whole belief rests on.

text: Removing the holding removes the influence rather than relocating it to a spouse, a partnership or a post-office job.
bottom_line: The weakest load-bearing part, and the one that caps the page.

text: A holdings ban can be enacted and enforced against sitting members.
bottom_line: Much stronger than it was two years ago, and still unfinished.

text: Reducing conflicts is worth a narrower candidate pool and a real compliance burden.
bottom_line: A value judgment that the cost-benefit table prices rather than settles.

text: Officials respond to financial incentives the way other people do.
Disclosure alone is sufficient when it is actually enforced.
Both sides want officials who are not, and do not appear to be, for sale.

Bar individual stocks, sector funds and derivatives for the official, spouse and dependent children; keep diversified funds and Treasuries legal; allow deferral of capital gains on forced divestiture; and set the penalty at a share of the transaction rather than a flat fee.
bottom_line: The most defensible version on offer; its weakness is political, not analytical.

text: The advertised reason is not what actually drives the position: Stop officials from trading on what they learn in office.
The advertised reason is not what actually drives the position: Protect ordinary property rights.
The people who would be bound are the people who must vote for it.
Opponents cannot point to a benefit of officials owning individual stocks that a diversified fund does not provide.
Scandal salience: a handful of vivid cases stands in for a rate nobody has measured.
Self-interest and status quo bias among the officials who would be bound.
The STOCK Act of 2012 made insider trading law explicitly applicable to Congress and required transaction reports within 45 days.
The Courthouse Ethics and Transparency Act of 2022 applied the same transaction reporting to federal judges and created a searchable database.
The criminal conflict-of-interest statute does not apply to the president, the vice president, members of Congress or federal judges.
bottom_line: Listed on the weakening side because it is cited that way; the linkage page is where that gets tested.

text: Citizens keep their ordinary rights when they take public office.
Senior executive branch officials and their spouses should be barred from holding individual stocks.
Congressional staff with access to nonpublic information should face the same ban.
Members of Congress should be barred from owning any asset other than Treasury securities and diversified funds while in office.
Members of Congress should be required to place individual stocks in a qualified blind trust.
Senators Jeff Merkley, Josh Hawley and Jon Ossoff have sponsored or cosponsored legislation to ban congressional stock trading.
Representatives Chip Roy and Seth Magaziner have sponsored the leading House bills in the 119th Congress.
Speaker Nancy Pelosi said in December 2021 that members should be able to participate in the free-market economy, before later supporting floor consideration of a ban.
bottom_line: Accurate as a quotation, misleading as a summary of her final position.

text: The anti-nepotism statute stops at the White House door, so the rule does not reach the place where the stakes are highest.
bottom_line: The legal gap is real and was formally relied upon; whether a court would agree has never been tested.

text: A relative cannot be supervised, disciplined or fired the way another official can, so the ordinary checks on an official's conduct do not operate.
bottom_line: The strongest argument on the page: it names a mechanism that does not depend on anyone's motives.

text: An official role gives a family member a channel that foreign governments and business partners can use, with the family's private interests attached to it.
bottom_line: Concrete and current; the rebuttal points at a narrower remedy.

text: The rule already applies to every other federal agency, so extending it closes a gap rather than inventing a restriction.
bottom_line: True, and the rebuttal reframes the whole proposal as an enforcement question.

text: Formal appointment is what brings a relative inside the ethics rules; a bar pushes the same influence outside them, where nothing applies.
bottom_line: The best argument against, and it is answered only if the rule is drafted around function rather than title.

text: The problem people actually point to is relatives trading on the family name in private business, which this proposal does not touch.
bottom_line: A genuine scope objection: the proposal is aimed at a smaller target than the grievance that motivates it.

text: A president is entitled to advisers he trusts, and Congress's power to tell him whom he may consult is constitutionally contested.
bottom_line: Strong for White House staff, weak for Senate-confirmed posts.

text: Competence is neither inherited nor disqualified by relation, and a blanket bar excludes people for a relationship rather than for a conflict.
bottom_line: Answers an argument the proposal does not make.

text: The Justice Department concluded that the federal anti-nepotism statute does not bar a presidential relative's appointment to the White House Office.
bottom_line: Authoritative in practice, untested in court.

text: Relatives by marriage have held Senate-confirmed and envoy positions outside the White House Office, including an ambassadorship in 2025 and a special envoy designation in February 2026.
bottom_line: Current and verifiable; the confirmation point cuts against reading it as an unchecked practice.

text: Relatives who became federal employees filed public financial disclosures reporting assets of up to roughly $762 million, with multiple amendments adding previously omitted holdings.
bottom_line: The concrete form of the "inside the rules" argument.

text: Federal candidates paid a combined $1.3 million in wages to people sharing their surname in one election cycle, entirely through campaign committees that no official-duty rule reaches.
bottom_line: Shows where the money actually moves, which is not where the proposal points.

text: After a bar takes effect, no relative of a president or a member holds a White House, envoy or ambassadorial post.
bottom_line: Easy to measure and easy to satisfy without changing anything, which is the objection in one line.

text: Documented contacts in which a foreign government routes business through a presidential relative fall relative to the preceding decade.
bottom_line: The right thing to measure, measured by a proxy that moves for other reasons.

text: Relatives continue to shape policy as private citizens and unpaid informal advisers, and the number of documented family-channel contacts is unchanged.
bottom_line: The way this belief most plausibly fails.

text: Official decisions stop being made by people the president cannot supervise or remove in the ordinary way.
Foreign governments lose a contact point that carries private family interests with it.
Career staff can raise objections to a senior adviser without raising them to the president about his own family.
A president loses advisers he trusts most, at some cost to the quality of advice he acts on.
Qualified people are excluded from public service for a family relationship they did not choose.
Influence moves to informal channels that file nothing and leave no record.
A relative in an official role creates conflicts that ordinary supervision and ethics rules cannot check.
bottom_line: Contested, and the disagreement is the mirror image of the "inside the rules" argument.

text: A bar removes the influence rather than pushing it into informal channels.
bottom_line: Tied for weakest load-bearing component on this page, which is why the cap bites.

text: Congress can impose the bar on White House appointments.
bottom_line: More defensible than the pardon case and less settled than the stock case.

text: Both sides want relatives' financial interests visible rather than hidden.

Bar relatives from Senate-confirmed and envoy positions, and require anyone performing official functions, whatever their title, to file the same disclosures and follow the same conflict rules as an employee.
Relatives of the president should be barred from Senate-confirmed positions but permitted to serve as unpaid advisers subject to full disclosure.

A return shows what the financial disclosure form does not: exact income and its character, foreign income and foreign tax credits, business losses carried forward, charitable giving, and the rate actually paid.
standalone: A published tax return shows what the federal financial disclosure form does not: exact income and its character, foreign income and foreign tax credits, business losses carried forward, charitable giving, and the rate actually paid.
bottom_line: The factual claim about what each document contains is correct; whether the extra content is what screens conflicts is the argument.

text: The internal check failed in the one case that tested it: the mandatory presidential audit was dormant, and the audit of the first two years opened the day Congress asked for the returns.
standalone: The internal check on a president’s tax compliance failed in the one case that tested it: the mandatory presidential audit was dormant, and the audit of the first two years opened the day Congress asked for the returns.
bottom_line: The strongest evidence on the page, and it is about the audit rather than about publication.

text: Every president from Carter through Obama released returns voluntarily, so a requirement restores a forty-year norm rather than inventing an obligation.
standalone: Every president from Carter through Obama released tax returns voluntarily, so a publication requirement restores a forty-year norm rather than inventing an obligation.
bottom_line: Accurate history; the step from norm to statute is the contested part.

text: A published return can be checked by anyone, which is the only enforcement that does not depend on an agency the official appoints.
standalone: A published tax return can be checked by anyone, which is the only enforcement of an officeholder’s tax compliance that does not depend on an agency the officeholder appoints.
bottom_line: The structural argument, and the one least dependent on any particular administration.

text: A return shows tax positions, not conflicts, and the disclosure form already lists assets, income sources, liabilities and positions in categories built for conflict screening.
standalone: A tax return shows tax positions, not conflicts, and the federal financial disclosure form already lists assets, income sources, liabilities and positions in categories built for conflict screening.
bottom_line: The best argument against, and the rebuttal is specific enough to test.

text: Publication exposes spouses, children and business partners who never ran for office.
standalone: Requiring the president and members of Congress to publish their tax returns would publish the finances of spouses, children and business partners who never ran for office.
bottom_line: A real privacy cost with a partial drafting answer.

text: The route is constitutionally narrow: a disclosure condition on ballot access was already struck down once, and a badly drafted rule would be litigated rather than obeyed.
standalone: The constitutional route to a tax-return publication requirement is narrow: a disclosure condition on ballot access was already struck down once, and a badly drafted rule would be litigated rather than obeyed.
bottom_line: The precedent is real and much narrower than the argument treats it.

text: Sophisticated wealth sits in pass-through entities and trusts that file their own returns, so a personal return can be published and show very little.
bottom_line: The most technically substantive objection on the page.

text: The mandatory IRS audit of presidential returns was "dormant, at best," and the audit of the 2015 and 2016 returns opened on April 3, 2019, the day the committee requested them; only 2016 was completed in office.
bottom_line: The dates are documentary and the characterization is the committee's.

text: Nixon released his returns in December 1973 and asked the Joint Committee on Taxation to review them; the review found roughly $465,000 in back taxes owed.
bottom_line: The founding case of the norm, and it cuts slightly against compulsion.

text: The public financial disclosure form already requires assets, income sources, liabilities, positions, agreements and gifts, reported in value ranges.
bottom_line: Accurate, and the range structure is exactly what the other side points at.

text: A state law requiring five years of returns from presidential primary candidates was struck down unanimously on state constitutional grounds.
bottom_line: Frequently cited for more than it holds, which is what its linkage page is for.

text: Within two election cycles of a publication requirement, at least one significant undisclosed foreign income source or lender relationship is found in a published return.
bottom_line: Diagnostic, and its failure would be ambiguous between deterrence and nothing to find.

text: Published returns add nothing to what the disclosure form already showed, and no conflict is identified from a return that the form had not already flagged.
bottom_line: Directly testable against the one case where both documents exist.

text: Foreign income and lender relationships become visible without a subpoena.
standalone: If the president and members of Congress published their tax returns, foreign income and lender relationships would become visible without a subpoena.

text: Voters can judge an official's financial entanglements before voting rather than after an investigation.
standalone: If the president and members of Congress published their tax returns, voters could judge an official’s financial entanglements before voting rather than after an investigation.

text: The audit of the president stops depending on an agency the president appoints.
standalone: If the president published their tax returns, the audit of the president would stop depending on an agency the president appoints.

text: Spouses, children and business partners have their finances published without holding office.
standalone: Under a tax-return publication requirement, spouses, children and business partners have their finances published without holding office.

text: Officials structure their finances to look unremarkable rather than to be efficient.
standalone: Under a tax-return publication requirement, officials structure their finances to look unremarkable rather than to be efficient.

text: Returns are read as scandal rather than as data, and complex but lawful items are litigated in public.
standalone: Published tax returns are read as scandal rather than as data, and complex but lawful items are litigated in public.

text: Tax returns contain conflict-relevant information that the financial disclosure form does not.
bottom_line: The most checkable component on any of these four pages.

text: Publication changes what officials do, or lets someone act on what it shows.
standalone: Publishing the tax returns of the president and members of Congress changes what officials do, or lets someone act on what it shows.
bottom_line: The weak link in substance, and it scores level with the other two rather than below them.

text: A federal publication requirement for officeholders can be enacted and would survive review.
bottom_line: Stronger than the pardon case: the disclosure precedent is well established.

text: Both sides want conflicts visible; they disagree about which document shows them.
Require exact values rather than ranges on the disclosure form, add foreign income and lender identity, and require the president to publish returns while leaving members under the enhanced form.
All senior federal officials, including agency heads and judges, should publish their tax returns annually.
Clemency is the only executive power with no check at all: impeachment reaches the officer, not the act, and the act is final the moment it is signed.
bottom_line: Structurally accurate. Whether the absence of a check is a defect or the point is the whole argument.

text: Pardons granted to the president's relatives, donors, business partners and co-defendants are the clearest case of office used for private benefit, and nothing reviews them.
bottom_line: The pattern is documented across parties, which is what makes it a structural argument rather than a partisan one.

text: A two-thirds threshold means only the pardons that both parties find indefensible would ever be reversed.
bottom_line: The threshold argument cuts both ways, and the page should show that rather than resolve it.

text: Most states already put a structural check on clemency and those systems function.
bottom_line: The best evidence that a check is workable, and the rebuttal correctly identifies that it is not this check.

text: Article II grants the power without a congressional role, and the Supreme Court has held it is not subject to legislative control, so this requires a constitutional amendment rather than a statute.
bottom_line: Decisive against a statute and not against the belief as written, which is why it is a component question rather than a refutation.

text: Clemency exists to correct injustices the political branches will not, so a legislative veto would remove precisely the unpopular mercy the power is for.
bottom_line: The strongest argument on the page in principle, and the two-thirds threshold is a real answer to it.

text: A reversible pardon is not a pardon: nobody could rely on it, and the power to settle whole classes of cases through amnesties would end.
bottom_line: A serious design objection with an obvious drafting answer that no proposal has adopted.

text: A narrower fix reaches the actual abuse without touching the power: prosecute bribes paid for pardons, and require the review file to be published.
bottom_line: The most practical alternative, and the response is that it has never actually been used.

text: 58 percent of Americans said the president grants too many pardons and 56 percent supported a constitutional amendment limiting the power, with Democrats at 76 percent and Republicans at 34 percent.
bottom_line: Real support, and the crosstabs are the reason to doubt the amendment path.

text: A federal judge unsealed a redacted opinion describing a Justice Department investigation into an alleged bribery-for-pardon scheme; no names were released and nobody was charged.
bottom_line: Enough to show the risk is not hypothetical; not enough to show it materialized.

text: Independent boards hold or gate the clemency power in more than a dozen states, and those systems operate continuously.
bottom_line: Strong precedent for a check; weak precedent for this particular check.

text: The Supreme Court held that the pardon power is not subject to legislative control and that Congress can neither limit the effect of a pardon nor exclude any class of offenders from it.
bottom_line: Decisive on the mechanism and silent on the belief as stated.

text: Proposals to let Congress nullify pardons by two-thirds vote have been introduced with bipartisan sponsorship and have not moved out of committee.
bottom_line: Listed on the weakening side because it is argued that way, and its linkage page is where the relevance fails.

text: In the decade after an override mechanism exists, the share of clemency grants that bypass the Justice Department review process falls.
bottom_line: The best-measured prediction on the page.

text: The override is never used, because two thirds of both chambers cannot be assembled against a president whose party holds a third of either one.
bottom_line: The most likely outcome, and the deterrence rebuttal is real but unmeasurable.

text: Presidents shift to pre-emptive and blanket pardons issued on the last day, where an override vote arrives after the recipients have scattered.
bottom_line: Predicts the adaptation, and names the drafting fix in its own rebuttal.

text: Pardons granted to the president's own circle become reviewable rather than final.
The prospect of a vote deters the grants that could not survive one.
Clemency decisions return to the Justice Department review process that screens petitions on the merits.
Unpopular but just clemency becomes harder, which is the case the power exists for.
Recipients cannot rely on a pardon, so it settles nothing until the override window closes.
Every controversial clemency decision becomes another partisan floor fight.
Some pardons are granted for the president's private benefit.
bottom_line: The pattern is documented and the characterization is inference. It is the firmest of the three components.

text: A congressional override would deter or reverse the grants at issue.
bottom_line: The weakest load-bearing component on this page, and the one that caps it. The prediction table says why.

text: An override mechanism can be enacted.
bottom_line: Argued down more effectively than the constitutional objection is usually argued, and not the component that caps this page.

text: Both sides agree that selling a pardon is a crime and that nobody currently checks whether one was sold.

Require the Pardon Attorney's file and the president's stated reasons to be published for every grant, and let Congress reverse a grant within sixty days by two-thirds vote, adopted as a constitutional amendment.
The pardon power should be abolished and replaced with a clemency commission whose decisions the president may only ratify.
A president should be barred from pardoning relatives, donors and co-defendants, with no general override.
Citizens need government decisions made on the merits rather than on what enriches the decider.
measured_by: Share of official decisions made by an official holding a personal financial stake in the outcome
if_true: Falls after the rule takes effect
latest: Not measured systematically; 78 members of one Congress filed late transaction reports (Insider, 2023)
bottom_line: Near the top of any hierarchy of public needs, and contested only at the edges of its application.

text: Investors need markets where nobody trades on information the government has not released.
measured_by: Abnormal returns on officials' trades placed before government announcements
latest: Mixed: 85 basis points a month for senators over 1993 to 1998 (Ziobrowski 2004); no advantage found over 2012 to 2020 (Belmont 2022); 3 to 5 percent before legislative events over 2014 to 2021 (Zhou 2025)
bottom_line: Valid and recognized; the disputed part is how much is actually at stake.

text: Voters need enough information to judge whether an official is compromised.
measured_by: Share of an official's income sources, debts and foreign ties visible in public filings
latest: Assets and income are disclosed in broad ranges; foreign income, lender identity and effective tax rate are not (OGE Public Financial Disclosure Guide, 2024)
bottom_line: Strong as a need, contested in how far into a family it reaches.

text: Crime victims and the public need clemency decisions that can be reviewed rather than traded.
measured_by: Share of clemency grants that went through the Justice Department review process
latest: About 93 percent of one administration's first-term grants bypassed the Pardon Attorney (Goldsmith and Gluck, 2020)
bottom_line: A real need with an unusually direct constitutional obstacle, which is argued on the belief page rather than here.

text: Officials need rules they can follow without a lawyer and without violating them by accident.
measured_by: Number of inadvertent reporting violations per year
latest: 78 members of the 117th Congress filed late under the STOCK Act (Insider, 2023)
bottom_line: Valid and usually ignored, and it is the interest a bright-line ban serves best.

text: Officials and their families need the same property rights and privacy as other citizens.
measured_by: Whether a restriction reaches only the official or also family members who hold no office
if_true: Restrictions stay narrow and are compensated
if_false: Restrictions extend to family and are not
latest: Proposals vary: most reach the spouse and dependent children, and the Federal Reserve rule reaches immediate family
bottom_line: Valid in general, weakest exactly where it is invoked most: a voluntary office with known conditions.

text: Large companies should be required by law to give their workers seats on their boards.
bottom_line: Whether the people whose jobs depend on a company have a stronger claim to steer it than the people whose money does.

text: Workers bear the costs of bad decisions such as layoffs and plant closures, so they deserve a voice in making them.
Workers know how the company actually runs day to day, and boards make better decisions with that knowledge in the room.
A board that answers only to shareholders tends to chase short-term stock gains at the expense of the company's long-term health.
Owners put their money at risk, and the people who bear the financial risk should be the ones who control the company.
Worker directors face a conflict of interest whenever the board must cut jobs or close a site to keep the company alive.
Boards with two sets of loyalties reach decisions more slowly, and slow companies lose to faster rivals.
A company generally serves the public best when it focuses on making a profit for its owners within the law.
bottom_line: Whether profit within the law is a good enough stand-in for public benefit or leaves too much harm uncounted.

text: Profit is a signal that a company is making something people want at a price they will pay, which is itself a public service.
Managers who are told to serve everyone end up answering to no one and can excuse poor results as serving some other goal.
Broad social problems are the job of elected governments, which answer to voters, not of managers who answer to no voter.
Many of a company's costs, like pollution or worker burnout, fall on people who never agreed to bear them and never show up in the profit figure.
The law always lags behind business practice, so a company that does only what the law requires will harm people the law has not yet caught up with.
Companies that treat workers, suppliers and towns well tend to earn trust that pays off over decades, which a narrow focus on profit misses.
Streaming services generally pay working musicians too little to make a living from recorded music.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the right comparison is with the old record business or with the obscurity most musicians faced before it.

text: A single play earns almost nothing, so only artists with enormous audiences see meaningful income from their recordings.
The money is split so that most of it flows to labels, publishers and the platforms before any reaches the person who wrote or performed the song.
Musicians now depend on touring and merchandise to survive, which favors the young and healthy and pushes out those who cannot live on the road.
Streaming brought paying listeners back after years of free downloading, and total music income has grown again as a result, spread across far more artists.
Before streaming, most musicians earned nothing from recordings because they never got a record deal at all, so the comparison is with obscurity, not with a golden age.
Low per-play rates reflect what listeners will pay for unlimited music, and forcing rates higher would shrink the audience rather than raise incomes.
Streaming has clearly done more good than harm for musicians by letting anyone reach a worldwide audience without a record label.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether being able to publish anywhere is worth much when so many others can too.

text: Any musician can upload a song and be heard anywhere in the world the same day, which was impossible when labels controlled distribution.
Listeners discover artists from other countries and small scenes, so careers can start from anywhere instead of a few music-industry cities.
Artists keep the rights to their own work more often, because they no longer need a label's money to press records and ship them to stores.
When everyone can publish, the flood of new songs makes it harder than ever for any one artist to be noticed, and reach without attention is worth little.
Playlists chosen by platform staff and software have replaced record labels as gatekeepers, so artists still depend on a few decision-makers they cannot reach.
Making music available for almost nothing worldwide has taught listeners that music should cost nothing, and that expectation follows artists into every other part of their business.
Comedians should generally be able to joke about any subject without losing work over the offense a joke causes.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether losing bookings over a joke is censorship or simply the market answering back.

text: Comedy works by saying what people are not supposed to say, and a comedian who must avoid every touchy subject cannot do the job.
Audiences already control comedy by laughing or not, and a joke that lands badly punishes itself without anyone needing to end a career.
When comedians are punished for offense, the safest response is blandness, and the loss falls on every audience, not just the people who were offended.
Losing a booking is not censorship; venues and networks are free to decide who they pay, just as comedians are free to speak.
A joke that spreads contempt for a group is a public act with public consequences, and the person who makes it should answer for it like anyone else.
Great comedians have always worked within limits set by their audience and era, and doing so pushed them toward sharper and more original material.
Jokes that mock people for their race, religion, disability or sex do real harm and deserve public pushback.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a joke about a group targets the stereotype or the people, and on who gets to say which.

text: Laughter makes contempt feel normal, so a joke can spread an ugly attitude further than a plain insult ever could.
People in the mocked group hear the joke too, and being the punchline in a room full of laughter teaches them they do not belong.
Pushback is itself free speech; a comedian who claims the right to offend cannot deny others the right to answer.
Most jokes about groups poke at the stereotype rather than the people, and audiences understand the difference better than critics assume.
Comedians from within a group often tell the sharpest jokes about it, and a blanket rule against such jokes silences them first.
Organized pushback rarely stays with the worst offenders; it quickly reaches mild jokes and creates a fear that shrinks comedy for everyone.
Traditional publishers still generally produce better books for readers than self-publishing does.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a publisher's filter selects for quality or merely for what it expects to sell.

text: A publisher's editors, designers and fact-checkers catch problems an author working alone cannot see, and readers get a cleaner book as a result.
Publishers pay authors in advance, which lets writers spend a year or more on a book instead of rushing out whatever sells fastest.
When a publisher has to invest its own money in a book, it must judge whether the book is worth a reader's time, and that judgment filters out a great deal of weak work.
Publishers pick books they think will sell, not books that are good, so their filter favors the familiar and rejects much that readers would love.
Online reviews and recommendations now do the sorting that publishers once did, and they do it with far more readers weighing in.
Self-published authors can hire the same editors and designers publishers use, so the quality gap comes down to money, not to who owns the imprint.
Most working authors are better off self-publishing than signing with a traditional publisher.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether keeping most of each sale outweighs losing guaranteed money and access to stores, libraries and reviewers.

text: A self-published author keeps most of each sale, while a traditional contract hands the publisher the larger share for the life of the book.
Authors who self-publish keep control of their rights, pricing and cover, and can fix mistakes or change course without asking permission.
Publishers put their marketing behind a few lead titles each season, and most authors on their lists get little more than a listing in a catalog.
Self-publishing turns a writer into a small business owner who must handle editing, design, marketing and taxes, and most writers are neither good at that nor want to be.
Bookstores, libraries, prizes and review pages still mostly deal with traditional publishers, so self-published books are shut out of the places where readers browse.
An advance is guaranteed money in a field where most books lose money, and a self-published author carries every cost and every risk alone.
Governments should generally require proven childhood vaccines for school attendance.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether protecting the classmates who cannot be vaccinated outweighs a parent's right to decide for their own child.

text: Some children cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons, and they are only protected when nearly everyone around them is.
Schools gather many children in close quarters every day, which is exactly the setting where an outbreak spreads fastest.
A requirement tied to school attendance reaches almost every family, while a purely voluntary approach leaves gaps that a disease can find.
Parents, not school administrators, are responsible for a child's body and should make medical decisions for that child.
Mandates breed resentment and distrust of public health, which can lower vaccination rates over time more than persuasion would.
Most vaccine-preventable diseases are already rare, so the added benefit of forcing the last holdouts is small compared with the cost to liberty.
Routine cancer screening of healthy adults with no symptoms generally does more harm than good.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the lives saved by catching a few cancers early outweigh the worry, tests, and treatment inflicted on the many who were never going to be hurt by what was found.

text: Screening finds many slow-growing abnormalities that would never have caused harm, and treating them exposes healthy people to surgery and drugs they did not need.
A false alarm sets off follow-up tests and weeks of fear, and false alarms are common when large numbers of people who feel fine are tested.
Finding a cancer earlier often just means a person lives longer knowing they have it, without changing when or whether they die from it.
Many cancers are far easier to treat before they spread, and screening is the only way to catch them in people who feel fine.
Patients can be told the risks of overdiagnosis and choose for themselves; the answer to false alarms is better counseling, not fewer tests.
The harms of screening are mostly temporary anxiety and minor procedures, while the harm of a missed cancer is death.
Adults should generally be allowed to buy common prescription drugs from a pharmacist without a doctor's visit.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the doctor's visit before a routine prescription is a safeguard worth its cost or a toll booth.

text: Many prescriptions are refills of medicines a person has taken for years, and requiring an appointment to renew them adds cost and delay without adding safety.
Pharmacists are trained in drugs and their interactions, often more thoroughly than the doctors who prescribe them.
People who cannot easily get to a doctor, because of cost, distance, or work hours, often go without medicine they need rather than jump through the hoops.
A doctor's visit catches problems the patient did not come in for; the refill is often the excuse that gets a person examined at all.
Pharmacists work for stores that profit from selling drugs, which puts them in a poor position to tell a customer not to buy one.
Antibiotic resistance and dependence on some medicines grow when access loosens, and those harms fall on everyone, not just the buyer.
Governments should generally set a maximum price for medicines that are still under patent.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the money saved today is worth the medicines that might not be invented tomorrow.

text: A patent already gives a company a monopoly, and a monopoly seller with sick customers will charge whatever the desperate will pay unless someone stops it.
Much of the basic research behind new drugs is paid for by taxpayers, so the public has already bought a share of the result.
Patients who skip doses or split pills because of cost end up sicker and in hospitals, and that bill lands on everyone.
Companies invest in research because a successful drug earns a large return; cap the return and the riskiest, most valuable research is the first to be cut.
A cap set by officials will be wrong in both directions, too high for cheap-to-make drugs and too low for hard ones, because no committee knows the true cost of discovery.
Prices are already bargained down by insurers and public programs; a legal cap adds a blunt tool where negotiation is already doing the work.
California should generally override local zoning rules to force far more housing to be built.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the housing shortage is caused by local vetoes that only the state can break, or whether state mandates fail to deliver homes on their own.

text: Local governments have blocked new homes for decades because existing residents vote and future residents cannot, and only the state answers to both.
Teachers, nurses, and service workers commute for hours because they cannot afford to live near their jobs, and that cost falls on the whole state.
People and businesses are leaving the state mainly because of housing costs, which shrinks the tax base that pays for everything else.
Local communities understand their own roads, schools, water supplies, and fire risks, and homes added without regard to those limits create new problems.
State mandates have mostly produced lawsuits, paperwork, and resentment rather than finished homes, because building still depends on local approval in practice.
Market-rate construction alone does not produce housing that low-income families can afford, so the state's effort would be better spent on direct subsidy.
Texas should connect its separate electric grid to the national grids rather than keeping it apart.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the reliability gained from sharing power across regions is worth giving up state control over how the grid is run.

text: When extreme weather hits, a connected grid can import power from regions that are not suffering the same storm, which is exactly when a closed grid fails.
Texas produces more wind and solar power than it can always use, and connection would let it sell that surplus instead of wasting it.
Investors are more willing to build power plants and transmission lines where they can reach a bigger market.
Connecting to the national grids brings federal oversight of prices and rules, and the state's freedom to run its own market is the reason it has been able to build so much new generation so quickly.
The lines needed to connect the grids would cost an enormous amount and take many years, and the state can harden its own system faster and cheaper.
Neighboring regions have had their own blackouts and shortages, so connection would not guarantee help in a crisis and could import their problems.
Judging teachers partly by their students' test results generally makes schools better.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether test results measure what a teacher actually adds or mostly reflect which students walked in the door.

text: Without a measure of results, teacher ratings rest on a principal's impression, and nearly everyone ends up rated the same.
Parents deserve to know whether their child's teacher is helping students learn, and test growth is the one measure that can be compared across classrooms.
Teachers who consistently help students grow deserve recognition and pay that a system without measurement cannot give them.
Students arrive with wildly different home lives and prior learning, and a single year's scores cannot cleanly separate the teacher's effect from everything else.
When jobs depend on scores, teaching narrows to what is tested, and subjects, projects and habits that are not tested get pushed aside.
Strong teachers avoid the hardest schools and classes when a low score can cost them their job, which hurts exactly the students who need them most.
Teachers generally do their best work when they control what and how they teach rather than following a set script.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the average classroom is better served by an expert's plan applied faithfully or by a teacher's on-the-spot judgment about the children in front of them.

text: A teacher sees each child's confusion in real time and can change course, while a script written far away cannot.
Professionals who are trusted stay in the job longer, and turnover harms students more than any curriculum choice.
Lessons a teacher believes in are taught with an energy that students notice, and scripted lessons rarely earn that belief.
Most teachers were never trained to design a curriculum, and asking each one to build their own means many students get an untested plan.
Well-designed materials carry the judgment of many experts, and a teacher who follows them gives students a better lesson than most could write alone.
Children who move between classrooms and schools need continuity, and full teacher control means what a child learns depends on luck.
Statues honoring historical figures who did serious wrongs should generally be removed from public squares.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a public statue is an honor that the living may withdraw or a record that the living have a duty to keep.

text: A statue in a public square is an honor paid by the community, not a history lesson, and a community is entitled to stop honoring someone whose deeds it now finds shameful.
Public spaces belong to the people who use them now, and asking them to walk past a tribute to someone who harmed their ancestors is a daily insult they never agreed to.
Moving a statue to a museum with an explanation preserves the history better than leaving it on a pedestal with no context at all.
Removing monuments makes the uncomfortable parts of the past easier to forget, and a society that cannot see its old heroes clearly cannot learn from its old mistakes.
Nearly everyone honored in the past fails some test of the present, so a rule of removal has no natural stopping point and ends up emptying the squares.
Decisions about which statues fall become contests of political power rather than judgments about history, and each side then tears down what the other side put up.
Historians generally should not judge people of the past by today's moral standards.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether understanding a past era requires setting aside our moral views or whether refusing to judge is itself a moral choice.

text: People in the past could not know what later generations would learn, and blaming them for not seeing it is like blaming a doctor of an earlier century for not using medicine that had not been invented.
The historian's job is to explain why people acted as they did, and moral condemnation tends to replace that explanation with a verdict that teaches nothing.
Our own standards will look wrong to our descendants in ways we cannot predict, so the humility we would want from them is the humility we owe the past.
In nearly every era there were people who objected to the cruelties of their time, which shows the alternatives were visible and the choice to ignore them was a real choice.
Declining to judge is not neutral, because a history told without moral weight quietly tells readers that the suffering of the victims did not much matter.
History is written for the living, and readers need to know not only what happened but whether it was right, or the past cannot guide anything they do next.
Fish clearly feel pain in a way that matters, not just a reflex to avoid harm.
bottom_line: It comes down to whether behaving as if hurt is enough to conclude that something is felt, or whether a mammal-like brain is required.

text: Fish have the nerve structures and chemical messengers that carry pain signals in mammals, so the machinery for feeling pain is present.
Fish change their behavior for a long time after an injury, including avoiding places where they were hurt, which a simple reflex would not produce.
Pain relief drugs return injured fish to normal behavior, which is what you would expect if the injury was being felt rather than just detected.
Fish lack the outer brain layer that in mammals turns damage signals into conscious suffering, so the signals may never become an experience.
Avoiding a place where you were hurt can be learned without any feeling, as simple machines and insects already show.
Judging an animal's inner life from behavior that looks like ours projects human experience onto a creature built very differently.
Claims that apes and parrots understand language generally reflect human wishful thinking rather than real ability.
bottom_line: The disagreement is about where understanding begins: at using a sign for something absent, or only at building new sentences.

text: Trained animals mostly produce signs or words when a reward follows, which is what you would expect from learned tricks rather than from meaning.
The people reporting an animal's language use are usually the ones who raised and love it, and they read intention into ambiguous signs.
No animal has been shown to combine signs into new sentences with grammar, which is the part of language that separates it from a vocabulary of signals.
Some animals use learned signs to ask for things that are not present, which shows the sign stands for an idea and not just a trained response.
Wild animals already use different calls for different dangers and answer accordingly, so a foundation for meaningful communication exists without any human trainer.
Demanding full human grammar before counting anything as understanding sets a bar designed so that only humans can clear it.
Most people with depression or anxiety would clearly benefit from professional treatment rather than handling it on their own.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether common sadness and worry are illnesses that need expert care or ordinary struggles that most people can and should work through themselves.

text: Trained therapists and doctors have methods that work and that a person cannot easily apply to themselves, just as a person cannot set their own broken bone well.
The very symptoms of depression, low energy and hopelessness, make self-help unlikely to succeed, because the illness attacks the will needed to fight it.
Untreated problems tend to grow, affecting work, family, and physical health, so early professional care prevents larger costs later.
Sadness and worry are normal responses to hard lives, and calling them illnesses teaches people they are broken when they are simply struggling.
Many people recover fully through exercise, sleep, friendship, and time, and steering them all toward clinics uses up limited care that the severely ill need.
Treatment carries its own risks, including medication side effects and dependence on a therapist, that are worth accepting only when the problem is serious.
Teaching children to build toughness and tolerate discomfort does more for their mental health than teaching them to monitor and talk about their feelings.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether paying close attention to feelings makes children stronger by helping them ask for help or weaker by making small worries loom large.

text: Constant attention to feelings can make small worries seem large, and children who learn to push through discomfort discover they can handle more than they feared.
Life will bring hardship that no amount of talking can prevent, so the skill that lasts is the ability to keep going through it.
Children who are treated as fragile tend to act fragile, while children expected to cope generally rise to the expectation.
Children who cannot name what they feel cannot ask for help, and telling them to tough it out teaches them to hide problems until they become crises.
Toughness training works for children who are already secure, but for a child who is being bullied or abused it means suffering in silence.
Talking about feelings and building toughness are not opposites; naming a fear is often the first step to facing it.
Tariffs on imported goods generally cost a country's consumers more than they save its workers.
bottom_line: Whether a small cost spread across everyone is worse than a large cost concentrated on the towns and workers who lose.

text: A tariff raises the price of the good for every buyer in the country, while it protects only the workers in one industry.
Other countries answer tariffs with their own, so exporters in industries that were never in trouble lose their foreign customers.
Industries shielded from foreign competition tend to stop improving, so the country ends up paying more for worse products.
When a factory closes, a whole town can lose its tax base, its shops and its future, and that damage is far larger than a small price increase spread across everyone.

When a tariff is removed, importers and retailers often keep much of the price difference for themselves rather than passing it on, so the saving that reaches shoppers is smaller than the wages that were lost.
A country that lets its factories die loses the skills and supply chains it would need in a war or a crisis, and no price saving is worth that.
A country should protect its key manufacturing industries with tariffs even when imports are cheaper.
bottom_line: Whether the goods a country cannot afford to lose can be identified honestly and protected more cheaply than with a tariff.

text: A country that cannot make its own steel, chips or medicine is at the mercy of whoever does, and that is a matter of security rather than price.
Manufacturing jobs offer steady middle-class pay to people without college degrees in a way that few service jobs do.
New industries need time to grow before they can compete with established foreign rivals, and a tariff buys that time.
Every industry calls itself key when a tariff is on offer, so protection ends up going to whoever lobbies hardest rather than to what a country truly needs.
Manufacturers who use the protected good as an input pay more, so protecting one industry weakens the ones that depend on it.
A country that wants secure supply can stockpile goods or fund a few plants directly, which costs far less than taxing every buyer.
Raising the minimum wage generally helps low-paid workers more than it hurts them.
bottom_line: Whether employers respond to a higher wage floor mostly by paying more or mostly by hiring less.

text: A single worker has almost no power to bargain with a large employer, and a wage floor gives them the bargaining position they lack.
Low-paid workers spend nearly everything they earn, so higher wages flow straight back into local businesses.
When wages are too low to live on, taxpayers end up topping them up through public benefits, which is a subsidy to low-paying employers.
When labor costs more, employers hire fewer people, cut hours or turn to machines, and the workers who lose out are the least skilled.
Small businesses in poorer regions cannot pay what a big-city employer can, so one national floor destroys jobs where they are most needed.
Many minimum-wage earners are young people or second earners in comfortable households, so a higher minimum wage misses the poorest families it is meant to help.
Employers should generally be free to fire workers without having to show a reason, as long as the firing is not discriminatory.
bottom_line: Whether making firing easy creates more jobs than it makes worse.

text: An employer who knows firing will be hard is slower to hire in the first place, so strict rules protect people who have jobs at the expense of people who want them.
Small businesses cannot afford the lawyers and paperwork needed to build a case for every dismissal.
Workers can quit a job without giving a reason, so fairness requires that employers be able to end the same working relationship without giving one.
Losing a job can mean losing a home, health coverage and a family's stability, and something that serious should require a reason.
Workers who can be fired at any moment are afraid to report safety problems, harassment or fraud.
Rules against unfair dismissal push employers to hire more carefully and manage better, which improves the workplace for everyone.
Internet providers should generally be barred by law from speeding up, slowing down or charging extra for particular websites and services.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether competition and public attention are enough to keep providers honest, or whether the lack of choice in home internet makes a legal rule necessary.

text: A provider that can slow down or charge extra for certain traffic gains a veto over which websites and services succeed, and that power belongs with users, not with the company selling the connection.
Many households have little real choice of home internet provider, so competition alone cannot punish one that plays favorites.
New services start small and cannot pay for fast lanes, so a rule of equal treatment keeps the door open for the next useful idea.
Not all traffic is alike; a live video call suffers far more from delay than a file download does, and a legal ban on favoring traffic turns sensible prioritizing into a legal risk.
Building faster networks costs a great deal, and letting providers charge the services that send the most traffic for faster delivery helps pay for upgrades that all users share.
Providers rarely block or throttle in practice because customers and the press notice quickly, so the rule solves a problem that mostly does not occur.
Laws that require people to prove their age before using social media do more harm than good.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the privacy and access costs of checking everyone's age outweigh the harm to children the checks are meant to prevent.

text: Proving age means handing an ID or a face scan to a company or a middleman, which creates a new store of sensitive data that can leak or be misused.
Teenagers who are blocked from mainstream sites do not stop going online; they move to smaller, less moderated places where the risks are greater.
Age rules set by law sweep in adults too, since everyone has to pass the same check, so a protection for minors becomes a barrier for all.

Society already requires proof of age for alcohol, gambling and driving, and there is no principled reason that products children use heavily and that are built to hold their attention should be exempt.
Leaving the choice to parents has not worked, because a child needs only one friend with an account to feel left out, and parents cannot supervise every hour.
Companies can verify age without keeping the underlying documents, but voluntary adoption has been patchy and inconsistent, which is why a uniform legal requirement is needed.
We should support and strengthen democracy to restore the voter's voice.
bottom_line: The problem diagnosis is strong: current electoral rules let unrepresentative primary electorates pick the choices, let mapmakers pick their voters, and make candidates depend on a narrow donor class. The reform mechanisms are less certain, since each specific fix (ranked-choice voting, nonpartisan primaries, commissions, donor matching) has real supporting evidence and real implementation risks, so this belief is strongest as "fix the structures, state by state, and measure" and weakest as a blanket endorsement of any one mechanism.

text: Partisan primaries let a small and unrepresentative group of voters pick the choices everyone else gets in the general election.
Gerrymandering lets legislators choose their voters instead of voters choosing their legislators.
Ranked-choice voting produces winners with broader support and reduces negative campaigning.
Campaign finance structures make candidates dependent on a donor class whose interests differ from those of their constituents.
Third parties and independents are kept out by structural election rules, not because they are unpopular.
Specific electoral reforms have real implementation problems and unintended consequences.
The two-party system has stabilizing effects that alternative systems may not replicate.
Restoring the voter's voice assumes there is a single coherent will of the voters to restore, but on many issues public opinion contradicts itself.
Campaign finance restrictions collide with the First Amendment's protection of political spending as speech.
Nonpartisan primaries may weaken party accountability rather than strengthen the voter's voice.
Congress polls at 15 to 25 percent approval while incumbent reelection rates exceed 90 percent.
Primary voters measure significantly more ideologically extreme than each party's general-election supporters.
Americans identifying as independents reached 43 percent, more than either party, while remaining excluded from most primaries.
Alaska's first federal ranked-choice election showed none of the predicted voter confusion and had normal ballot-completion rates.
Independent redistricting commissions in Arizona and California reduced safe seats by 15 to 20 percent compared with maps drawn by legislatures.
Policy outcomes correlate with the preferences of economic elites at far higher rates than with the preferences of the median voter.

Burlington, Vermont adopted ranked-choice voting and then repealed it after the candidate with the most first-choice votes lost, though scholars dispute whether the result was actually unfair under the rules.
The evidence on whether nonpartisan primaries actually moderate candidates is mixed.
Independent voters, about 43 percent of Americans, need a meaningful vote because they are locked out of primaries.
Voters need representatives who solve problems rather than perform for their base audiences.
The Forward Party and other third parties need open primaries and ranked-choice rules because they benefit directly from them.
Opponents need governmental stability and coherent governing coalitions.
Voters need simple ballots and elections they can understand.
Incumbents and major-party organizations need to protect the rules that protect them, and donors need to protect their channel of influence.

A decade of data from Alaska and Maine will show that reformed states elect measurably more median-aligned representatives and that their approval-to-reelection gap narrows compared with matched unreformed states.
Legislators in jurisdictions with small-donor matching will track constituent preferences better than legislators in jurisdictions without it.
Commission-drawn maps will keep producing 15 to 20 percent fewer safe seats than maps drawn by legislatures, cycle after cycle.
Jurisdictions that use ranked-choice voting will show persistently lower rates of negative advertising.
Reformed states will show no movement on any objective criterion after two full election cycles, or repeal waves will spread beyond single incidents like Burlington.
Center-squeeze or other pathological outcomes will recur in ranked-choice elections at rates that measurably erode public trust in results.
Representatives in reformed states will move toward their district medians no faster than representatives in unreformed states.
Companies should need a person's clear permission before collecting their data for advertising.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether people can give meaningful consent to data collection at all, and on who should pay for the free services that collection now funds.

text: Information about a person belongs to that person first, and taking it without asking treats people as a resource rather than as customers.
Most people do not know how much is gathered about them or where it goes, so silent collection cannot be called consent in any real sense.
Requiring permission before collecting personal data forces companies to explain what they want and why, which by itself makes them collect less than they otherwise would.
Advertising pays for most free online services, and when fewer people opt in to data collection for ads, those services either start charging money or disappear.
Permission screens quickly become a wall of clicks that people wave through without reading, so requiring consent before data collection adds friction without adding understanding.
Ads matched to a person's interests are less annoying and more useful than random ones, and many people prefer them once they see the difference.
Law enforcement should be able to read encrypted messages when it has a warrant.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a way in for lawful searches can exist without becoming a way in for everyone else.

text: A warrant already lets police search a home or open a safe, and a message on a phone should not be more protected than a letter in a drawer.
People who plan serious harm use encrypted apps precisely because they know no one can look, and society should not build them a guaranteed hiding place.
Letting police read an encrypted message only after a judge finds there is cause keeps the decision to look with a court rather than with the officers who want to look.
There is no way to build a way into encrypted messages that only the police can use; any built-in opening can be found and used by criminals and hostile governments.
Warrants are issued in one country, but the same software runs everywhere, so a way in created for one government becomes available to all of them.
Ordinary people, businesses and journalists rely on encryption for their safety, and weakening it for everyone in order to catch a few makes the whole population less secure.
New movies should generally open in theaters for a period before they reach streaming services.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the shared theater experience is worth making everyone wait for it.

text: A theater run gives a movie a single shared moment when people talk about it, which builds interest that a quiet streaming release rarely matches.
Seeing a film on a big screen with a crowd is a different and richer experience, and a period when a new film is only in theaters is the only way to keep that as the default way to see a movie.
Theaters are local businesses that employ people and anchor downtowns, and they cannot survive if every film is available at home on the day it opens.
Families, rural viewers and people with disabilities find theaters costly or hard to reach, and a forced wait before new films reach home screens treats them as second-class audiences.
Piracy fills any gap between a movie's release and its availability at home, so delays mostly push viewers toward illegal copies.
Streaming lets small and unusual films find their audience without fighting for a limited number of screens, so a theater-first rule protects blockbusters more than it protects film as a whole.
Studios should let viewers choose to watch new movies at home on the same day they open in theaters.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether viewer convenience or the health of the theater business should decide where a new movie can be seen.

text: Viewers, not studios, should decide where they watch a film they are paying for.
Tickets, parking and babysitting make a night out expensive, and a home option puts new films within reach of people on tight budgets.
A same-day home release lets a film reach people who live far from any theater, so its audience grows instead of shrinking.
A same-day home release cuts theater attendance in the very weeks a film needs it most, and the lost ticket income is not replaced by streaming fees.
Movies watched at home compete with phones and interruptions, so filmmakers lose the focused attention their work was made for.
Once viewers expect every film at home on opening day, studios have less reason to spend on the large-scale pictures that only make sense on a big screen.
Cities should generally redesign streets to slow cars down, even when that lengthens drive times.
bottom_line: It turns on how many minutes of driving time a community will trade for fewer deaths and more people able to walk and bike.

text: Whether a crash kills someone depends mostly on speed, so a street built for slower driving saves lives without relying on drivers choosing to behave better.
Streets where cars move slowly are streets where children, old people and cyclists can safely be, which gives everyone a choice besides driving.
Redesigning a street to slow cars costs each driver a small amount of time on each trip, while the safety gained is shared by every person who uses the street.
Longer trips cost workers, deliveries and emergency vehicles real time every single day, and those costs add up across a whole city.
Slowing a main road pushes drivers onto neighborhood side streets, moving the danger to places that were quiet before.
In most places most people have no practical alternative to driving, so making driving worse punishes them without giving them a better option.
Banning the sale of new gasoline cars by a fixed date is generally a mistake.
bottom_line: It turns on whether a firm deadline speeds the industry up or outruns what buyers and the charging network can absorb.

text: Electric cars are still out of reach for many buyers, and people in apartments and rural areas often have nowhere to charge one.
